description: Heat is a form of energy that flows due to a temperature difference. Thermodynamics is the branch of physics that deals with the relationships between heat, work, temperature, and energy.

sections.title: Basics of Heat and Temperature
sections.description: Fundamental principles of heat and temperature, their units, and scales of measurement.

key_concepts.explanation: A form of energy that transfers from a body at a higher temperature to a body at a lower temperature. Its SI unit is the Joule (J).
The measure of the degree of hotness or coldness of a body. Its SI unit is the Kelvin (K).
The amount of heat required to raise the temperature of a unit mass (1 gram or 1 kg) of a substance by 1°C. Water has a very high specific heat capacity (4200 J/kg°C).

scientific_principles.application: Used to interconvert temperatures between Celsius (C), Fahrenheit (F), Kelvin (K), and Reaumur (R) scales.

sections.title: Transmission of Heat
sections.description: The different methods by which thermal energy is transferred from one place to another.

key_concepts.explanation: The transfer of heat in solids where energy is passed from molecule to molecule without the actual movement of the particles. Example: Heating a metal rod.
The transfer of heat in liquids and gases caused by the actual physical movement of the heated particles. Example: Boiling water, sea and land breezes.
The transfer of heat through electromagnetic waves without the need for any material medium. Example: Heat from the Sun reaching the Earth.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: The rate of heat loss of a body is directly proportional to the difference in temperatures between the body and its surroundings.
scientific_principles.application: Explains why a hot cup of coffee cools down faster initially and slower as it approaches room temperature.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: E ∝ T^4 (The total radiant heat energy emitted from a black body is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature).
scientific_principles.application: Used to estimate the temperatures of stars and the Sun.

sections.title: Laws of Thermodynamics
sections.description: Fundamental laws governing energy conservation and the direction of heat flow.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: If two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
scientific_principles.application: Forms the basis for the concept of temperature and the functioning of thermometers.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW (Heat supplied = Change in internal energy + Work done).
scientific_principles.application: An adaptation of the Law of Conservation of Energy. It is the operating principle behind heat engines.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: Heat cannot spontaneously flow from a colder body to a hotter body (Clausius statement).
scientific_principles.application: Governs the working of refrigerators and air conditioners, and introduces the concept of Entropy.

sections.title: Change of State and Latent Heat
sections.description: The transition of matter from one state to another and the energy involved in the process.

key_concepts.explanation: Melting point is the constant temperature at which a solid becomes a liquid. Boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas.
The direct transition of a substance from a solid state to a gas state without passing through the liquid phase. Examples: Camphor, Naphthalene, Dry Ice (Solid CO2).

The 'hidden' heat required to change the state of a substance without changing its temperature. The latent heat of fusion of ice is 80 cal/g, and the latent heat of vaporization of water is 540 cal/g.

sections.title: Measuring Instruments and Important Facts
sections.description: Crucial one-liner facts and scientific instruments related to heat measurement for exam preparation.

key_associations.extra_info: Used to measure the temperature of celestial bodies like the Sun (based on radiation).
Used for detecting and measuring the power of incident electromagnetic radiation.

important_facts.fact: The normal temperature of the human body is 37°C, which equals 98.6°F or 310 K.
At -40 degrees, both the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales register the exact same numerical value (-40°C = -40°F).
Water exhibits 'Anomalous Expansion': its maximum density and minimum volume occur at 4°C.
Absolute Zero is the lowest possible temperature where molecular motion ceases completely; it is equal to 0 K or -273.15°C.
Burns caused by steam are far more severe than those caused by boiling water at the same temperature due to the high latent heat of vaporization in steam.
